written.myAnswer: Homeostasis is the ability of an organism to maintain a stable internal environment despite changes in the external environment. It is important because cells function properly when internal conditions, such as temperature, pH, and the concentrations of salts, glucose, and oxygen, remain within their normal ranges.

When body temperature rises, the brain’s temperature-regulating centre signals the sweat glands to produce sweat. Evaporation of sweat removes heat and cools the body. When temperature falls, muscles shiver, generating heat and raising body temperature towards normal.

The digestive system breaks down food and makes nutrients available to the body’s cells for energy, growth, and repair. The excretory (urinary) system removes wastes and regulates water and salt balance, helping maintain stable internal conditions.

Homeostasis is the ability to maintain a stable internal environment despite external changes. It is important because cells need conditions such as temperature, pH, and concentrations of salts, glucose, and oxygen to remain within suitable ranges. The nervous and endocrine systems coordinate body activities. The respiratory system supplies oxygen and removes carbon dioxide; the cardiovascular system transports substances and helps regulate temperature and pH. The digestive system makes nutrients available, the urinary system removes wastes and regulates water and salt balance, and the integumentary system helps regulate temperature through sweating. These systems work together to maintain stable internal conditions.

The respiratory system brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide. The cardiovascular system transports oxygen to cells and carries carbon dioxide from them to the lungs for removal. During exercise, breathing and heart rates increase to meet the muscles’ greater oxygen demand and remove the extra carbon dioxide, helping maintain appropriate levels of both gases.

Organ systems work together to maintain homeostasis, allowing cells to function properly. For example, the respiratory system exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide, while the cardiovascular system transports these gases between the lungs and cells. If one system fails, other systems may not receive the substances or stable conditions they need; for example, respiratory failure reduces oxygen supply and impairs carbon dioxide removal. This disrupts other systems and can upset homeostasis.
